structure.title: 5. MFD as a Measure of Disagreement
Appendix A Control Variables; B MFD Construction; C Different MFD parameterizations

observations.statement: The empirical object is a cross-sectional return-prediction test: whether a simulated disagreement measure (dispersion of forecasts across randomly specified machine learning investor-models) predicts next-month stock returns. The design is stated as nonparametric portfolio sorts plus parametric Fama-MacBeth regressions.

A dedicated subsection motivates each modeling assumption of the belief simulator (sophisticated optimizing investors, high-dimensional information sets, tree ensembles) by citing prior empirical and experimental evidence, and the authors flag that the plausibility of the simulation distribution is a key question addressed by robustness to alternative distributions.
observations.locator: Introduction; Section 1.2 Motivation for modeling choices

observations.statement: The authors anticipate the objection that their distribution of model specifications may be biased in other ways than analyst surveys, and answer it by framing the method as a modifiable, complete methodology that other researchers can re-specify.

Stock characteristics and returns come from a publicly available replication dataset (Jensen, Kelly, Pedersen), with underlying CRSP and Compustat sources named; a footnote gives the GitHub location of that dataset and its code.

Sample is common stocks on NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ; financial and utility firms are excluded, and low-priced stocks are dropped with the stated justification of reducing the influence of small and illiquid stocks. Table notes repeat the SIC-based exclusion definitions.

The full data period and the shorter out-of-sample test period are stated separately; the gap is explained by the rolling estimation window used to train the investor models. Table notes restate the sample period, including shortened windows when a factor model or proxy is available only for part of the period.
Observation counts are printed per column in the Fama-MacBeth table and in the panel regression table, but not in portfolio-sort tables.

Mechanism tests use proprietary short-lending fee data from IHS Markit and 13F institutional holdings from Thomson Reuters, each with its own shorter availability window noted in the text or footnote.

The key variable is defined by equation as the cross-investor standard deviation of forecasts; the construction (number of investors, size of each information subset, random forest hyperparameters, rolling window, refit frequency, in-sample winsorization) is laid out in an appendix table, with a footnote noting the equal-weighted formulation differs from a related paper.
observations.locator: Equation (4); footnote 4; Section 2.1; Appendix B Table B1

observations.statement: All predictor characteristics are cross-sectionally rank-transformed each period and mapped to a bounded interval, following cited machine learning asset pricing papers.

Winsorization thresholds differ by use: summary statistics winsorize both tails at one level, regression controls at a tighter level and are standardized, and in-sample training returns are winsorized only in-sample, never out-of-sample.
observations.locator: Table 1 notes; Table 6 notes; Table 11 notes; Table B1 notes

observations.statement: Control variable definitions and their source papers are given in the Table 1 notes and again in an appendix table; alternative dependent variables (industry-adjusted and DGTW characteristic-adjusted returns) are defined in the text when introduced.
observations.locator: Table 1 notes; Section 3.4; Appendix A Table A1

observations.statement: Composite indices (a disagreement index and a limits-to-arbitrage index) are built by averaging or summing decile ranks of component proxies, following cited papers; the text and table note for the arbitrage index differ on the number of components.
observations.locator: Section 5.3; Figure 4 notes; Section 6.3; Table 16 notes
observations.note: Section 6.3 text lists three components; Table 16 notes list four including firm age.

observations.statement: The main portfolio table reports each decile and the high-minus-low spread with raw excess return and alphas from five factor models in adjacent columns, in separate equal-weighted and value-weighted panels, with Newey-West t-statistics in parentheses and significance stars.

The Fama-MacBeth table adds controls progressively across three columns, then swaps the dependent variable for industry-adjusted and characteristic-adjusted returns in two further columns; R-squared is not reported.

The panel regression table lists controls, entity and time fixed effects as Yes rows, reports observations and R-squared per column, and its note states the estimating equation, the clustering dimensions, and standardization of variables.

Portfolio weighting is stated for every sort: the headline sort reports both equal and value weights, while conditional sorts used for mechanisms are equal-weighted and the market-phase test is value-weighted.
A footnote states that all reported t-statistics are Newey-West adjusted with a fixed lag count to address heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation; the lag choice itself is not further justified.

Panel regressions for volume and volatility double-cluster by month and firm, and the earnings-announcement daily panel clusters by day following the cited source paper; no explicit reasoning for these cluster choices is given.
Differences in the return spread between high and low uncertainty states are tested with a one-sided t-test, stated in the table note, consistent with the directional hypothesis.

Before controlling for characteristics, the paper reports time-series averages of cross-sectional medians of firm characteristics across sorted deciles, using the pattern to motivate which controls are needed next.

A long section validates the new measure against existing proxies: distribution of monthly rank correlations with analyst dispersion (density figure), parallel Fama-MacBeth regressions of both measures on firm characteristics (bar figure), rank correlations with many other proxies, and a decomposition of a composite index.

Time-variation checks split the sample at the median of many aggregate uncertainty, sentiment and factor-density proxies and report the spread in each state and its difference in one table; a LASSO count of selected characteristics defines factor density.

A short robustness section summarizes in prose a battery of checks that live entirely in the Internet Appendix: persistence over horizons, extended bivariate sorts, a three-pass estimator robust to omitted factors, nonlinear SDF pricing errors, alternative ML architectures and hyperparameters, easy-to-predict stocks, international markets, and an earnings-based version of the measure.
observations.locator: Section 4; Internet Appendix A to H

observations.statement: Robustness of the measure to its own construction is shown in the main text by re-running sorts with four hyperparameter sets or four different learner types, tabulated as one row per configuration with configuration IDs keyed to an appendix table.
observations.locator: Section 5.6; Table 12; Appendix C Table C1

observations.statement: Bivariate dependent double sorts on each of twelve characteristics are compressed into a single table reporting only the spread and its alpha per control, with the note explaining that the full grid of portfolios is omitted for brevity.

Heterogeneity is delivered through conditional (dependent) tercile-by-quintile sorts on mispricing score, borrowing fee, institutional ownership and an arbitrage-cost index, each table pairing an average-characteristic panel with a spread panel and a difference-in-spreads row.

Mispricing versus risk is adjudicated by three steps: alphas across factor models, correlation with an existing mispricing score, and concentration of returns in earnings-announcement windows using a daily panel with an interaction term, following a cited protocol for locating announcement days by scaled volume.

The measure is decomposed into a model-disagreement part and an information-set part by re-expressing the belief equations with separate indices for model and information subset, then sorting on each component.

Panel regressions link the measure to contemporaneous and next-month trading volume and volatility as theory-implied consequences of disagreement, with the lagged dependent variable included for persistence.

Economic magnitude of the regression slope is translated by multiplying the average slope by the decile spread in the standardized regressor; panel coefficients are read in standard deviation units because both sides are standardized; the annualized spread and a comparison with the analyst-based measure anchor the headline.

The announcement-window effect is expressed as a percentage increase of the strategy spread relative to nonannouncement days, and state-dependent spreads are compared to the unconditional average from the main table.

The authors acknowledge that the simulated belief distribution may lack features other researchers deem important and present the framework as modifiable rather than definitive; they also note the measure is only as broad as the characteristics data available.

International replication across developed and emerging markets is presented explicitly as evidence of external validity, and the method is described as applicable to any asset class with characteristics data.

Tables use three-level significance stars with t-statistics in parentheses; every table note restates sample period, sort procedure, weighting and the standard-error adjustment; a summary statistics table and a rank-correlation table open the empirical part.

Figures include a rolling-average time-series plot of the aggregate measure against other aggregates, a density plot of monthly rank correlations with mean marked by dashed lines, an annotated bar chart of Fama-MacBeth slopes with t-statistics, and yearly median index ranks by portfolio rank.
Print appendices are lettered A to C with tables numbered A1, B1, C1; Internet Appendix material is referenced by letter sections and by I-prefixed figure and table numbers.

The introduction previews headline results with numbers and organizes the paper around three enumerated contributions (new measure, predictive power, economic underpinnings); there is no separate roadmap paragraph, but Section 5 opens with a subsection-by-subsection roadmap.

Order is model of beliefs, then data, then main sorts and regressions, then a short robustness section pointing to the Internet Appendix, then measure validation, then mechanisms, then conclusion; the print paper keeps only three small appendices and relies heavily on the Internet Appendix.
Footnotes carry substantive supplementary analyses (an earnings-announcement test for the long leg, definitions of the mispricing score and institutional ownership) rather than only citations.

A Code and Data Availability statement after the conclusion gives a Harvard Dataverse DOI for replication code and data; a footnote separately points to the public GitHub source of the input characteristics dataset. No software is named in the text.

Core inputs are public-use (published characteristics dataset built on CRSP and Compustat); mechanism tests draw on commercial sources (IHS Markit fees, Thomson Reuters 13F, StockTwits, option data) and a third-party-provided mispricing score acknowledged in the front matter.
The front matter carries a disclaimer for an author's affiliation with an investment management firm, stating views are the authors' own.

gaps: No justification given for the Newey-West lag length beyond citing the correction
No reasoning offered for the clustering dimensions in panel regressions (month and firm; day)
No multiple-testing adjustment discussed despite many sorts, proxies and market-phase splits
No software or package versions named in the paper text
R-squared and mean of the dependent variable not reported for Fama-MacBeth tables
Number of stocks per decile or per month not reported
Internet Appendix not available in the text file; its contents are known only from the prose summary in Section 4

reading.note: Pages 1 to 46 read in full (main text, Tables 1 to 16, Figures 1 to 4, print Appendices A to C). Pages 47 to 51 are the reference list and were only skimmed for headings. The Internet Appendix is not part of the text file.
